key_claims: The Haqqani network has been more important to the development and sustainment of al-Qa'ida and the global jihad than any other single actor or group.
The Haqqani network functions as a nexus player, tying together diverse actors across local, regional and global jihad.

The Haqqani network and al-Qa'ida function as an interdependent system, and the seeds of global jihad were planted earlier than previously thought and nurtured as much by the Haqqanis as by al-Qa'ida.
Loya Paktia and Miranshah were more central to al-Qa'ida's operational development than Peshawar and have proved more enduring.

The Haqqani network is a semi-autonomous component of the Taliban with primacy in southeastern Afghanistan, and has long had close ties to the Pakistani Army and intelligence agencies, which have used it as a proxy.
The Haqqani network is the primary conduit for many TTP fighters into Afghanistan and a central diplomatic interface between the TTP and the Pakistani state.
Haqqani leadership is hierarchical and mostly familial, centered on Jalaluddin, his brother Khalil and his sons, with non-family leaders such as Jan Baz Zadran and Mullah Sangeen.
The Haqqani network was recognized as a distinct tanzim by foreign jihadists by 1994 and was protecting al-Qa'ida's Khost camp from Hekmatyar-aligned attacks.
The Haqqani network's endurance rests on geographic centrality in Loya Paktia and North Waziristan.
Roughly a third of mujahidin supplies routed via Khost passed through Haqqani's Zhawara base.
The Haqqanis act as a hub: both Pakistan and al-Qa'ida are partners, and Islamabad and the TTP rely on their good offices.
The Taliban rely on the Haqqanis as the local face in Loya Paktia and as a force multiplier, especially in Kabul.
Pakistan has long sponsored the Haqqanis as a proxy, including against India.
The network avoids public association with anti-Pakistan militancy or global jihad through segmented communications.
The Haqqani network maintains its nexus position by providing a platform linking local, regional and global militant partners while masking each party's inputs.
Haqqani fronts facilitated al-Qa'ida's formation and the intermingling of fighters, contributing to TTP–al-Qa'ida ideological convergence.
Haqqani-controlled Paktia, not Peshawar, was where international mobilization became global jihad; bin Ladin's camps sat on Haqqani supply lines.
Jalaluddin Haqqani preceded 'Azzam in calling for individual duty to support the Afghan jihad and had means to facilitate it.
The ISI directed the Haqqani network's tactical operations in 1988-1992, and Zhawara was its coordination hub.
The Haqqani network avoids open association with global jihad or anti-Pakistan militancy despite ties to al-Qa'ida and TTP.
Zhawara functioned as a military academy: Arabs bound for al-Qa'ida's Ma'sada camp first trained with the Haqqani network.
The name al-Qa'ida derives from Bin Ladin's Jaji camp, which was structurally integrated with Haqqani operations.
Al-Qa'ida's early camps (al-Faruq, Jihadwal, Siddiq) near Zhawara trained agents of major 1990s attacks.
The 1991 capture of Khost integrated foreign fighters under Haqqani command, including Arab commanders.
The Haqqani-al-Qa'ida alliance persisted and internationalized after Bin Ladin moved to Sudan.
Jalaluddin and Nezamuddin Haqqani promoted an anti-US global jihad line in the early 1990s.
Haqqani camps at Zhawara trained Kashmiri, Central Asian, Arab and other militants, integrated with HuM/HuA and later al-Qa'ida.
Haqqani's joining the Taliban gave ISI another avenue of influence over Mullah Omar's movement.
Al-Qa'ida relied on Haqqani autonomy in Loya Paktia to issue declarations of war on the West, defying Mullah Omar.
The 1998 World Islamic Front announcement was staged in Haqqani-controlled Khost, not Kandahar.
After 9/11 the nexus of militants moved to North Waziristan under Haqqani sanctuary.
Al-Qa'ida's anti-American jihad was launched from Haqqani-controlled territory, making operation outside it prohibitive for foreign jihadis before 9/11.
After the 2001 invasion, foreign militants fled to the Haqqani refuge in North Waziristan rather than the Taliban's Baluchistan.
Haqqani-al-Qa'ida ties survived the leadership transition from Jalaluddin to Sirajuddin and are now multi-generational.
